# llm.asm

**Three complete LLM projects written in 100% pure x86-64 NASM assembly.**
Zero C, zero C++, zero Rust, zero libc, zero libm, zero runtime dependencies.

Assembled directly with `nasm` and linked with `ld`. Every math kernel (`expf`, `sincosf`, `RMSNorm`, `RoPE`, `SiLU`, `Softmax`), AVX2+FMA+F16C GEMM/GEMV engine, BPE tokenizer, `clone()`/`futex()` thread pool, bare-metal SMP kernel, analytical backward pass, AdamW optimizer, and live Unicode Braille TUI is hand-written x86-64 assembly (`17,252` lines total across all three projects).

## The Trilogy

| Project | Binary | Size | Deps | Key Numbers |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **[01-qwen3-inference/](01-qwen3-inference/)** | `build/asm-llm` | **14,712 B** *(14,008 B `FAST_Q8=0`)* | **0** | Static Linux ELF running `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` (Q8_0, built-in BPE tokenizer, GQA + QK-Norm + RoPE + SwiGLU, single-shot & `--chat` multi-turn KV-cache REPL). **`FAST_Q8=1` (default):** **126.8 tok/s** decode at 40T (**20.7 tok/s** at 1T), **+18% to +36% faster than `llama.cpp` CPU (`Q8_0`) across 1..40T**, **`0.99965`** cosine & **64/64** exact greedy tokens vs PyTorch FP32. |
| **[02-baremetal-os/](02-baremetal-os/)** | `build/asm-llm-os.elf` | **24,252 B** *(23,612 B `FAST_Q8=0`)* | **0** | Bootable bare-metal `Qwen3-0.6B` OS with no Linux or Windows. Multiboot 1 -> Long Mode -> AVX2/FMA/F16C -> ACPI/APIC SMP -> VGA + PS/2 + COM1 multi-turn KV-cache chat (`/clear`, `/think`, `/bench`). **74–94 ms** boot, **134.9 tok/s** KVM EPYC (**23.7 tok/s** 1 vCPU, **136.6 tok/s** peak), **55.4 tok/s** live on Proxmox Xeon E5-2670 v3 with **0 GB** disk. |
| **[03-minigpt-train/](03-minigpt-train/)** | `build/asm-gpt-train` | **32,944 B** | **0** | From-scratch FP32 Mini-GPT trainer and sampler. Register-blocked `6x16` AVX2+FMA SGEMM, full analytical backward pass (**`1.0000000000`** cosine across all 21 gradient tensors vs PyTorch CPU), decoupled AdamW, **27,662 train tok/s**, live 80x24 Braille TUI, `val_loss 4.19 -> 1.51` on TinyShakespeare in 4 min. |

---

## Head-to-Head CPU Decode Benchmark: `llm.asm` vs `llama.cpp` (`Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0`)

Measured on the same machine (**AMD EPYC 7642**, 47C online, 256 MiB L3, DDR4, CPU-only `-ngl 0`), same model (`Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0`: `613.66 MiB` `.asmbin` v2 FP16-scale vs `604.15 MiB` GGUF `Q8_0`), `34` prompt tokens / `64` generated tokens, `3`-run average:

| Threads | `llm.asm` (`FAST_Q8=0`, FP32 act) | `llama.cpp` (`Q8_0`, `-ngl 0`) | **`llm.asm` (`FAST_Q8=1`, 14.7 KB)** | **vs `llama.cpp`** | **Bare-Metal OS KVM (`FAST_Q8=1`)** |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **1** | 7.18 tok/s | 16.63 tok/s | **20.70 tok/s** | **1.24x (+24.5%)** | **23.67 tok/s** |
| **4** | 28.12 tok/s | 51.08 tok/s | **69.24 tok/s** | **1.36x (+35.6%)** | **78.89 tok/s** |
| **8** | 53.09 tok/s | 80.79 tok/s | **103.64 tok/s** | **1.28x (+28.3%)** | **118.08 tok/s** |
| **16** | 77.50 tok/s | 103.03 tok/s | **121.86 tok/s** | **1.18x (+18.3%)** | **134.94 tok/s** |
| **24** | 91.88 tok/s | 104.11 tok/s | **123.72 tok/s** | **1.19x (+18.8%)** | **132.90 tok/s** |
| **32** | 96.63 tok/s | 103.82 tok/s | **122.51 tok/s** | **1.18x (+18.0%)** | **133.75 tok/s** |
| **40** | 98.50 tok/s | 105.08 tok/s | **125.86 tok/s** *(peak 126.81)* | **1.20x (+19.8%)** | — |

*(Note: `llama.cpp` uses batched GEMM for prompt prefill `pp34`, whereas `llm.asm` runs token-by-token GEMV. For autoregressive decode `tg64`, `llm.asm` (`FAST_Q8=1`) combines INT8xINT8 AVX2 `vpmaddubsw`/`vpmaddwd`, `.asmbin` v2 FP16 block scales (`F16C vcvtph2ps`), monotonic next-row prefetch, contiguous head-major KV-cache, and parallel GQA attention — beating `llama.cpp` by +18%..+36% across 1..40 threads while producing bit-exact deterministic outputs across all thread counts. The bare-metal OS gains another ~10% from 2 MiB huge-page identity mapping.)*

## Quick Start

Clone the repo and build everything with `make all`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alesha-pro/llm.asm.git
cd llm.asm
make all
```

### 1. Run Qwen3-0.6B Inference in 14 KB (`01-qwen3-inference/`)

```bash
# Export compact .asmbin v2 (FP16 block scales, 613.66 MiB; or --scale-dtype fp32 for legacy v1)
python3 scripts/export_weights.py --model-dir models/qwen3-0.6b-bf16 --out models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin --scale-dtype fp16
# Build with FAST_Q8=1 (default: INT8xINT8 AVX2 + parallel GQA) or FAST_Q8=0 (exact FP32 activations)
make inference FAST_Q8=1
./build/asm-llm -m models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin -p "Explain how a CPU cache works in 3 concise sentences." -n 128 -t 16
# Or start an interactive multi-turn chat preserving the KV-cache across turns:
./build/asm-llm -m models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin --chat -t 16
```

Full step-by-step setup, model download, CLI flags, and benchmarks: **[01-qwen3-inference/README.md](01-qwen3-inference/README.md)**.

### 2. Boot Bare-Metal Qwen3-0.6B OS in 24 KB (`02-baremetal-os/`)

```bash
make os FAST_Q8=1
make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16
# Or build a bootable BIOS+UEFI ISO for QEMU / Proxmox VE:
make os-iso MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin
```

Full QEMU KVM, bootable ISO, and 0 GB disk Proxmox VE deployment guide: **[02-baremetal-os/README.md](02-baremetal-os/README.md)**.

### 3. Train Mini-GPT from Scratch in 32 KB (`03-minigpt-train/`)

Zero Python required to train or run inference:

```bash
mkdir -p data checkpoints && curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt -o data/tinyshakespeare.txt
make train
./build/asm-gpt-train --data data/tinyshakespeare.txt --steps 400 --seq 128 -t 16 --save checkpoints/shakespeare.ckpt
```

Full training, live Braille TUI, checkpoint chat loop, and PyTorch gradient check guide: **[03-minigpt-train/README.md](03-minigpt-train/README.md)**.

## System Requirements

- **CPU:** x86-64 with **AVX2 + FMA + F16C** (Intel Haswell / AMD Excavator or newer).
- **Build tools:** `nasm` and GNU `binutils` (`ld`, `objcopy`).
  ```bash
  sudo apt install nasm binutils
  ```
- **Phase 1 & 3 runtime:** Any Linux x86-64 kernel. Zero shared libraries (`readelf -d` reports no dynamic section).
- **Phase 2 runtime (optional):** `qemu-system-x86_64` with KVM, or any x86-64 hypervisor/bare-metal machine (Proxmox VE, VirtualBox, real hardware). Building bootable ISOs uses `grub-mkrescue` (`grub-pc-bin`, `grub-efi-amd64-bin`, `mtools`, `xorriso`).
- **Offline tooling (optional):** `python3` + `numpy` only for one-time `Qwen3-0.6B` `.asmbin` export and reference verification (`torch` + `transformers` only if running PyTorch parity checks).

---

## Architecture & Verification Summary

Every phase is built on the same engineering rules: no runtime libraries, deterministic parallel partitioning, and numerical verification against independent Python/PyTorch references.

- **Shared assembly core (`shared/`):** Phase 2 compiles the exact same `math.asm`, `matmul.asm`, `tokenizer.asm`, and `transformer.asm` with `-DBARE_METAL` (swapping Linux `mmap`/`clone`/`write` for physical Multiboot modules, APIC spin-barriers, and VGA+COM1 drivers). Phase 3 reuses `syscalls.asm` and `math.asm`.
- **Phase 1 verification:** All math/SIMD kernels pass unit tests within `1e-7..1e-6` (`init_rope_freqs` FP64 `< 5e-14`) for both `FAST_Q8=1` and `FAST_Q8=0` across v1 FP32 and v2 FP16 scale formats. `FAST_Q8=1` matches PyTorch FP32 `Qwen3-0.6B` with `cosine = 0.9996517` and **64/64 exact greedy tokens** (`FAST_Q8=0` matches the Python Q8_0 reference with `cosine = 1.000000000`). Bit-exact deterministic from `1T` to `40T`.
- **Phase 2 verification:** **100% token-exact and byte-for-byte identical** to Phase 1 across 5 test prompts (English, Russian UTF-8, arithmetic, `--think` mode), multi-turn KV-cache recall + `/clear`, and across `1..32` KVM vCPUs (`134.9 tok/s` at 16 vCPUs). Verified on both QEMU KVM (AMD EPYC 7642) and a real Proxmox VE VM (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 0 GB disk, BIOS GRUB ISO).
- **Phase 3 verification:** Verified against PyTorch FP32 CPU on all **21 parameter tensors** (`worst max_abs_diff = 3.35e-8`, `min cosine_sim = 1.0000000000`), 10-step AdamW + cosine LR + grad-clip trajectory (`max_loss_diff = 4.77e-7`), and bit-exact determinism across `1T`, `8T`, and `16T`.

See each project's README for full tables, memory layouts, and reproduction steps:

items.readme:
Stream Tube

A native YouTube client for Windows and Linux, written in Rust.
No browser, no ads, no tracking. SponsorBlock, DeArrow and Return YouTube Dislike built in.

## Why I wanted YouTube on my desktop without keeping a browser tab open, and without the ads, autoplaying junk and sponsor reads. The existing options were either Electron apps that eat a gigabyte of RAM or web frontends that break every other week. Stream Tube is a single native app: the UI is drawn on the GPU with [GPUI](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/tree/main/crates/gpui), and video goes through libmpv, so it starts fast and scrolls smoothly even with big feeds. ## What it does **No ads, anywhere** - No pre-roll, mid-roll or overlay ads: the app plays the video stream directly, so YouTube's ads are never loaded - No promoted videos, banners or sponsored cards in Home, search or Shorts - Sponsor reads inside videos are skipped too, with SponsorBlock (below) - Nothing to install or keep updated: it isn't an ad blocker that YouTube can break, ads simply aren't part of how the app plays video **Watching** - Home, Shorts, Subscriptions, Explore categories, channels (including their courses and shows), and playlists - Search with filters, suggestions, recent searches and more results as you scroll - A personal Home without an account: "For you" recommends videos related to what you've watched and searched in the app, mixed with new uploads from your subscriptions. Signed in, Home is your own YouTube Home feed - A *Recently uploaded* chip on Home, like youtube.com's: videos from your Home feed and subscriptions uploaded in the last two weeks, newest first - Hover a video title in a grid or list to read the full title - Ctrl+click a link or middle-click a video to open it in a background tab. A video's menu also has *Open in new tab*. Switch with Ctrl+Tab, Ctrl+1…9 or a click. Ctrl+T opens a new tab. Ctrl+W or a middle click on the tab closes it. - Videos made for kids (YouTube Kids) play and download like any other video - Old video annotations are back: notes, speech bubbles and clickable links from YouTube's annotation archive, drawn over the video where they used to be (turn them off in *Settings → Player* or from the player's gear menu) - Arabic, Hebrew and other right-to-left text is shown in the right order - Shorts follow your account's recommendations when you're signed in, or start from the Shorts you watched last - Download the current Short from the vertical player's download button - libmpv player with hardware decoding, codec preference (AV1, VP9 or H.264), 360p up to 4K, enhanced bitrate, speed control (remembered per channel if you want), captions you can style (font, colour, opacity, background and edge, with a live preview), chapters and seek-bar preview thumbnails - A chapters panel beside the player, like youtube.com: click the chapter name in the player bar (or *View all* under the description) to list every chapter with its thumbnail, follow the one playing, and jump to any of them - Timestamps in descriptions and comments seek the video and bring the player back into view - Resumes where you left off, remembers your last quality, autoplays the next video or loops, and plays whole playlists as a queue - Turn on *Original video titles* in Settings to show the creator's title when opening a video. - Hover over the video to step through available resolutions or adjust playback speed in 0.5× increments. Click the speed to reset it to 1×. - The picture-in-picture button opens the draggable in-app miniplayer or a floating window above other apps. Choose the mode in *Settings → Player*. Theater mode and fullscreen are also available, and the app remembers your theater setting. - Keeps playing when minimized, or pauses and resumes when you come back. On Windows, active video playback keeps the display awake. - Windows media controls can pause playback, resume it and move through the video queue. - On Windows, *Settings → General → Minimize to tray* keeps Stream Tube in the notification area when you minimize or close the window. Use the tray icon to reopen or quit the app. - Start *Cast over LAN* in Settings and open the temporary link on a phone on the same trusted network. If the desktop has more than one local address, choose the one on your phone's network. Paste a YouTube video link to play it on the desktop. - Turn on *Independent tab playback* and restart Stream Tube to play up to three tabs at once. Each tab keeps its own queue. Background tabs play audio, and a tab with a floating picture-in-picture window keeps showing video there. - Live streams with live chat (Top chat or every message), and chatting when signed in - Shorts in a vertical player that moves to the next one by itself, or open them in the regular player. Shorts comments open their replies as threads too - Hold Space or press and hold the main video to play at 2x - Press `+` / `-` or `>` / `<` to move to the next or previous 0.25x playback speed step - Hover previews: rest the pointer on a thumbnail and it plays inside it, muted, with a seek bar to skip around - Most replayed graph with "jump ahead", ambient glow around the player (on or off from the player's gear menu), force original audio instead of auto-dubbing - Aspect ratio controls for ultrawide screens, like the Ultrawidify extension: *Auto* finds a film's black bars and crops them away so it fills a 21:9 or 32:9 monitor, or pick 21:9, 18:9 or 32:9, *Zoom to fill* or *Stretch*. Choose it from the player's gear menu or *Settings → Player*, or press *Z* to cycle - A screenshot button in the player bar - Step one frame at a time with `,` or `.` while paused, or with Previous frame and Next frame in the player's right-click menu - Comments sorted by Top, Timed or Newest. *Timed* works like youtube.com: comments that mention a moment of the video appear as playback reaches it - Comments show animated GIFs, stickers and channel emojis, and replies are drawn as threads, with answers to a reply nested under it. Long comments and channel descriptions are shortened with *Read more* / *Show more* - Keyboard shortcuts for playback, seek, volume, captions, fullscreen, theater, picture-in-picture and the queue. Z changes the aspect ratio and Ctrl+←/→ changes chapters. Playback letter keys also work with the Russian layout. - Arrow keys briefly show the volume or the number of seconds skipped over the video - "Open in external player" with no setup: it uses VLC or mpv if one is installed, otherwise your default video player, and continues from where you were - Right-click the video for loop, copy link (optionally at the current time), screenshot and **Stats for nerds**: resolution, codecs, dropped frames, hardware decoding, bitrate, buffer health and connection speed, updated live (also *Shift+I*) **Saves data** - Audio only mode fetches just the audio stream, so podcasts, music and talks use a fraction of the data - Pick a lower default quality, and turn off hover previews or seek-bar thumbnails if you're on a metered connection **Premium features, free** - No ads, background play, picture-in-picture, downloads, jump ahead and enhanced bitrate all work without YouTube Premium and without signing in **Less noise** - SponsorBlock with per-category behaviour: skip automatically, ask, only mark it on the seek bar, or ignore - Use your own SponsorBlock private ID and see your contribution stats (segments, skips by others, time saved) - DeArrow titles and thumbnails, so you see what a video is actually about - Return YouTube Dislike counts - Hide Shorts, live streams, premieres, watched videos, comments, related videos, description, chapters, channel avatars, view counts and Explore - Block channels or keywords from every feed **Your data stays yours** - Subscriptions can live locally. The feed is built by fetching each channel directly, no account needed - Sign in with your Google account to get your own Home feed, subscriptions, playlists, likes and subscribe button. Stream Tube opens youtube.com/activate in your default browser with the sign-in code already filled in, so you only pick your account and allow access. Stream Tube imports your YouTube watch history and recent searches automatically after sign-in - Sign in to YouTube to open Watch later, Liked videos and any account Favorites playlist from the sidebar. The local playlists are available in Library. - Signed in, videos play through YouTube's TV client as your account: no "confirm you're not a bot" checks, and age-restricted videos play. The JavaScript puzzles in YouTube's stream URLs are solved with the scripts from [yt-dlp/ejs](https://github.com/yt-dlp/ejs) in a built-in QuickJS engine, or in [Deno](https://deno.com) or [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) when one is installed, which is a few times faster - Videos you watch in Stream Tube and the positions you stop at go back to your YouTube account through the same sign-in, so other devices resume where you left off. If you prefer, connect a browser session instead under *Settings → General → YouTube watch history*: sign in with a fresh browser profile (Chrome, Edge, Brave or Chromium) that is deleted afterwards, or load a `cookies.txt` file - Your YouTube watch history refreshes in the background and when you return to Stream Tube - History, watch later, favourites and playlists are stored in a local SQLite database, and you can pause or clear history at any time - Import from YouTube Takeout, NewPipe, FreeTube or OPML. Export to NewPipe JSON, YouTube CSV, OPML or a full backup **Downloads** - Download video or audio in any quality through yt-dlp, with SponsorBlock chapters, from a download manager with progress - Save a transcript as plain text (.txt) or timestamped subtitles (.srt) from the Download menu. A single caption track downloads immediately. If several tracks are available, choose the language; automatically generated tracks are labeled in the picker. - Without yt-dlp it falls back to the built-in downloader (360p/720p or audio) - yt-dlp and FFmpeg can be fetched from inside the app, on Windows and Linux (*Settings → Downloads*), with a progress bar, so nothing has to be installed by hand **Open from the browser** - The [Stream Tube userscript](userscript/stream-tube.user.js) adds an *Open in Stream Tube* button to youtube.com (or press Alt+S). The video continues in the app from where you were. Install it with Tampermonkey or Violentmonkey; it can also send every video to the app by itself - `streamtube://open?url=` links open the app, which is set up when you install it (or the first time the portable build runs) **Network** - A proxy setting (HTTP or SOCKS) that covers browsing, playback, thumbnails, downloads and sign-in - On Linux, a choice of Wayland or X11, with an automatic switch to X11 if a Wayland window never shows up (ChromeOS) - IPv4-only mode applies to new requests as soon as you change it. You can also choose a playback client (TV, visionOS, Android VR or yt-dlp). **Looks the way you like** - Dark, light or follow Windows - Seven accent colours used across the app, and the app icon changes colour to match, on the taskbar and on your desktop shortcuts too - Interface scaling, density, thumbnail corner style, grid columns, start page, language and region - English, Azerbaijani, French, German, Japanese, Kazakh, Russian, Turkish, Ukrainian, Simplified Chinese and Traditional Chinese in *Settings → General → App language*. YouTube has a separate language setting. - Smooth page, dialog and menu transitions, and mouse-wheel scrolling that glides instead of jumping - Scrollbars you can drag (shown on hover, or always), and pages scroll from the keyboard too: Page Up/Down, Home/End, the arrow keys and Space **Keeps itself up to date** - Checks for new releases at startup and installs them in one click, and can update yt-dlp for you. Every download is checked against its SHA-256 before it is used ## Performance Stream Tube versus youtube.com in Microsoft Edge (clean profile, no extensions) on the same Windows 11 PC, playing the same video. Numbers are the working set of every process involved, after browsing a few pages. | | youtube.com in Edge | Stream Tube 0.4.0-alpha | |---|---|---| | Processes | 11–12 | 1 | | RAM, idle on Home | 1,073 MB | **~405 MB** | | RAM, playing a video | 1,203 MB | **~565 MB** | Stream Tube uses less than half the RAM of the browser, and it stays flat as you browse: thumbnails are kept at the size they're drawn and the ones you've scrolled past are freed. While playing, part of the memory is a read-ahead buffer that keeps seeking instant. Turn on *Settings → Player → Hardware decoding* to decode video on the GPU like the browser does. Results depend on the video, resolution and hardware. ## Screenshots
Live streams with chat Search
Settings SponsorBlock and DeArrow

## Install Get the latest build from the [Releases page](https://github.com/Avaneesh-Inamdar/Stream-Tube-Desktop/releases). This is an early alpha, so expect rough edges. **Windows 10/11 (64-bit)**: run `StreamTube--setup.exe`. It installs for your user only, so no administrator prompt, and the app updates itself when a new release comes out (*Settings → About*). To run it without installing, choose *Extract All* on `StreamTube--windows-x64.zip`, then open `streamtube.exe` in the extracted folder with `libmpv-2.dll` beside it. It doesn't need the Visual C++ runtime. After you extract a build with portable update support, use *Settings → About* for future updates. Stream Tube replaces the app files in that folder and restarts with the same settings and history. Older PCs whose graphics driver has no Vulkan support (for example Intel HD 4000) work too: the app carries its own Vulkan loader for libmpv and uses it only when Windows doesn't have one. **Debian, Ubuntu, Mint**: install the `.deb`. This also installs libmpv: ```sh sudo apt install ./streamtube_0.7.5-alpha_amd64.deb ``` **Fedora, openSUSE**: install the `.rpm`: ```sh sudo dnf install ./streamtube-0.7.5-alpha.x86_64.rpm ``` **Any Linux (x86_64), nothing to install**: download the AppImage, make it executable and run it. libmpv is inside, so video plays without installing anything else: ```sh chmod +x StreamTube-0.7.5-alpha-x86_64.AppImage ./StreamTube-0.7.5-alpha-x86_64.AppImage ``` **Other Linux (x86_64), installed for your user**: unpack `StreamTube--linux-x86_64.tar.gz` and run `./install.sh`. It puts the app in `~/.local/bin` and adds a menu entry. Video plays through libmpv, so install it if you don't have it: ```sh sudo apt install libmpv2 # Debian 12+, Ubuntu 24.04+ (Ubuntu 22.04: libmpv1) sudo dnf install mpv-libs # Fedora sudo pacman -S mpv # Arch ``` **macOS (Apple Silicon), unofficial.** Releases may include a `StreamTube--macos-arm64-UNOFFICIAL.zip`. It is built from the [`community/macos-apple-silicon`](https://github.com/Avaneesh-Inamdar/Stream-Tube-Desktop/tree/community/macos-apple-silicon) branch, contributed by [William Wessex](https://github.com/wwessex). I don't have a Mac, so keeping that branch up to date and packaging it is done with the help of AI. It is **not tested on a real Mac by the maintainer** and isn't supported: use it at your own risk. It needs `brew install mpv`, and since it isn't notarised, macOS will warn before opening it. Downloads above 360p need yt-dlp and FFmpeg. The app offers to fetch both the first time you need them, on Windows and Linux, or get them any time from *Settings → Downloads*. You can also install them with your package manager instead. ### Verifying a download Every file on a release is built by the public [Release workflow](.github/workflows/release.yml) on GitHub's runners. Each release lists the files' SHA-256 checksums in `SHA256SUMS.txt`, and each file has a signed build provenance attestation that ties it to the workflow run that built it. With the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com): ```sh gh attestation verify StreamTube-0.7.5-alpha-setup.exe --repo Avaneesh-Inamdar/Stream-Tube-Desktop ``` Check a download against those before running it. The in-app updater also checks the installer's SHA-256 before running it. ## Building You need: - **Rust 1.85 or newer** (the crate uses the 2024 edition). Get it from [rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs). - **libmpv** — download a `mpv-dev-x86_64` archive from [shinchiro's mpv builds](https://github.com/shinchiro/mpv-winbuild-cmake/releases) and put `libmpv-2.dll` in `third_party/mpv/`. It isn't in the repo because it's over 100 MB. - **yt-dlp** (optional, recommended) — on your `PATH`, or point to it in *Settings → Backend & network*. It's used for downloads and as a fallback when the built-in extractor can't get a stream. Then: ```powershell git clone https://github.com/Avaneesh-Inamdar/Stream-Tube-Desktop.git cd Stream-Tube-Desktop cargo build --release ``` The executable ends up at `target\release\streamtube.exe`. To run it somewhere else, copy `libmpv-2.dll` next to it. To build the installer, install [Inno Setup 6](https://jrsoftware.org/isinfo.php) and run: ```powershell ISCC.exe /DAppVersion=0.7.5-alpha installer\streamtube.iss ``` It lands in `dist\`. On Linux, install the packages listed in [`.github/workflows/linux.yml`](.github/workflows/linux.yml) and run `cargo build --release`. ## Where things are stored History and subscriptions go in `%APPDATA%\StreamTube\streamtube.db` on Windows and `~/.local/share/StreamTube/streamtube.db` on Linux. Settings (content filters, SponsorBlock choices and everything else) are kept in `settings.json` in the same folder, so they survive updates and signing out. If the database is ever damaged, it is rebuilt from what can still be read at the next start, and the damaged file is kept beside it. Set `STREAMTUBE_DATA_DIR` to keep everything somewhere else (for example a portable copy). If you used the app back when it was called Ferrotube, your old data is moved over automatically on first launch. ## Project layout ``` src/ api/ Innertube client, stream extraction, sign-in, SponsorBlock/DeArrow/RYD player/ libmpv binding, playback controller, player UI, local stream proxy ui/ app shell, pages (home, watch, shorts, settings, ...), cards, PiP window feed.rs local subscription feed import.rs Takeout / NewPipe / FreeTube / OPML import store.rs SQLite storage ``` ## Known issues - YouTube sometimes answers with "Sign in to confirm you're not a bot". Signing in inside the app avoids it; otherwise updating yt-dlp usually fixes it. - Windows is the main platform. The Linux build is new and less tested; macOS isn't built yet. ## Contributing Pull requests are welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to build, what makes a PR easy to merge, and what won't be accepted. ## Credits Stream Tube leans on a lot of other people's work: [mpv](https://mpv.io), [yt-dlp](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp), [SponsorBlock](https://sponsor.ajay.app), [DeArrow](https://dearrow.ajay.app), [Return YouTube Dislike](https://returnyoutubedislike.com), [GPUI](https://www.gpui.rs), [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org) and the annotation archive saved by [Archive Team](https://wiki.archiveteam.org/index.php/YouTube/Annotations). Thanks also to everyone who has sent fixes and features; each release's notes name who did what, and the full list is on the [contributors page](https://github.com/Avaneesh-Inamdar/Stream-Tube-Desktop/graphs/contributors). It's an independent project and isn't affiliated with or endorsed by YouTube or Google. ## License [MIT](LICENSE)
